vsm1.2:35.1: v. The one-sessioner’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse eating in several sessions”
vsm1.2:35.3: When the one-sessioner sits down in the sitting hall, instead of sitting on an elder’s seat,
vsm1.2:35.4: he should notice which seat is likely to fall to him and sit down on that.
vsm1.2:35.5: If his teacher or preceptor arrives while the meal is still unfinished, it is allowable for him to get up and do the duties.
vsm1.2:35.6:
But the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūla-Abhaya said: “He should either keep his seat and finish his meal or if he
gets up he should leave the rest of his meal in order not to break the ascetic practice.
vsm1.2:35.7:
And this is one whose meal is still unfinished; therefore let him do
the duties, but in that case let him not eat the rest of the meal.”
vsm1.2:36.2: Herein, one who is strict may not take anything more than the food that he has laid his hand on whether it is little or much.
vsm1.2:36.3: And if people bring him ghee, etc., thinking “The elder has eaten nothing,”
vsm1.2:36.4: while these are allowable for the purpose of medicine, they are not so for the purpose of food.
vsm1.2:36.5: The medium one may take more as long as the meal in the bowl is not exhausted;
vsm1.2:36.6: for he is called “one who stops when the food is finished.”
vsm1.2:36.7: The mild one may eat as long as he does not get up from his seat.
vsm1.2:36.8:
He is either “one who stops with the water” because he eats until he takes water for washing
the bowl, or “one who stops with the session” because he eats until he gets up.
vsm1.2:36.9:
The ascetic practice of these three is broken at the moment when food has been eaten at more
than one session. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:37.1: The benefits are these. He has little affliction and little sickness; he has lightness, strength, and a happy life;
vsm1.2:37.2:
there is no contravening rules about food that is not what is left over from a meal; craving for tastes
is eliminated; his life conforms to the principles of fewness of wishes, and so on.
vsm1.2:38.1:
No illness due to eating shall he feel
Who gladly in one session takes his meal;
No longing to indulge his sense of taste
Tempts him to leave his work to go to waste.
vsm1.2:38.2:
His own true happiness a monk may find
In eating in one session, pure in mind.
Purity and effacement wait on this;
For it gives reason to abide in bliss.
vsm1.2:38.3: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach, and benefits, in the case of the one-sessioner’s practice.
vsm1.2:39.1: vi. The bowl-food-eater’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse a second vessel”
vsm1.2:39.3: When at the time of drinking rice gruel, the bowl-food eater gets curry that is put in a dish;
vsm1.2:39.4: he can first either eat the curry or drink the rice gruel.
vsm1.2:39.5: If he puts it in the rice gruel, the rice gruel becomes repulsive when a curry made with cured fish, etc., is put into it.
vsm1.2:39.6:
So it is allowable to do this only in order to use it without making it repulsive.
Consequently this is said with reference to such curry as that.
vsm1.2:39.7: But what is unrepulsive, such as honey, sugar, etc.,
vsm1.2:39.8: should be put into it. And in taking it he should take the right amount.
vsm1.2:39.9: It is allowable to take green vegetables with the hand and eat them. But unless he does that they should be put into the bowl.
vsm1.2:39.10:
Because a second vessel has been refused it is not allowable to use anything else,
not even the leaf of a tree. These are its directions.
vsm1.2:40.2: Herein, for one who is strict, except at the time of eating sugarcane, it is not allowed while eating to throw rubbish away,
vsm1.2:40.3:
and it is not allowed while eating to break up rice-lumps, fish, meat and cakes. The rubbish should
be thrown away and the rice-lumps, etc., broken up before starting to eat.
vsm1.2:40.4: The medium one is allowed to break them up with one hand while eating; and he is called a “hand ascetic.”
vsm1.2:40.5: The mild one is called a “bowl ascetic”;
vsm1.2:40.6:
anything that can be put into his bowl he is allowed, while eating, to break up, that is, rice lumps,
etc., with his hand or such things as palm sugar, ginger, etc., with his teeth.
vsm1.2:40.7: The moment anyone of these three agrees to a second vessel his ascetic practice is broken. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:41.1: The benefits are these. Craving for variety of tastes is eliminated; excessiveness of wishes is abandoned;
vsm1.2:41.2:
he sees the purpose and the right amount in nutriment; he is not bothered with carrying saucers,
etc., about; his life conforms to the principles of fewness of wishes and so on.
vsm1.2:42.1:
He baffles doubts that might arise
With extra dishes; downcast eyes
The true devotedness imply
Of one uprooting gluttony.
vsm1.2:42.2:
Wearing content as if ‘twere part
Of his own nature, glad at heart;
None but a bowl-food eater may
Consume his food in such a way.
vsm1.2:42.3: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach, and benefits, in the case of the bowl-food-eater’s practice.
vsm1.2:43.1: vii. The later-food-refuser’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse additional food”
vsm1.2:43.3:
Now, when that later-food refuser has shown that he is satisfied, he should not again have the food made
allowable by having it put into his hands according to the rule for bhikkhus and eat it.
vsm1.2:43.4: These are the directions for it.
vsm1.2:44.2:
Herein, there is no showing that he has had enough with respect to the first lump, but there
is when he refuses more while that is being swallowed.
vsm1.2:44.3:
So when one who is strict has thus shown that he has had enough with respect to the second lump,
he does not eat the second lump after swallowing the first.
vsm1.2:44.4: The medium one eats also that food with respect to which he has shown that he has had enough.
vsm1.2:44.5: But the mild one goes on eating until he gets up from his seat.
vsm1.2:44.6:
The moment any one of these three has eaten what has been made allowable again after he has shown that he
has had enough, his ascetic practice is broken. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:45.1: The benefits are these. One is far from committing an offence concerned with extra food; there is no overloading of the stomach;
vsm1.2:45.2:
there is no keeping food back; there is no renewed search for food;
he lives in conformity with the principles of fewness of wishes, and so on.
vsm1.2:46.1:
When a wise man refuses later food
He needs no extra search in weary mood,
Nor stores up food till later in the day,
Nor overloads his stomach in this way.
vsm1.2:46.2:
So, would the adept from such faults abstain,
Let him assume this practice for his gain,
Praised by the Blessed One, which will augment
The special qualities such as content.
vsm1.2:46.3:
This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades,
breach, and benefits, in the case of the later-food-refuser’s practice.
vsm1.2:47.1: viii. The forest-dweller’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse an abode in a village”
vsm1.2:48.1: Now, that forest dweller must leave an abode in a village in order to meet the dawn in the forest.
vsm1.2:48.2: Herein, a village abode is the village itself with its precincts.
vsm1.2:48.3:
A “village” may consist of one cottage or several cottages, it may be enclosed by a wall or not, have human
inhabitants or not, and it can also be a caravan that is inhabited for more than four months.
vsm1.2:48.4:
The “village precincts” cover the range of a stone thrown by a man of medium stature standing between
the gate-posts of a walled village, if there are two gate-posts, as at Anurādhapura (cf. Vin III 46).
vsm1.2:48.5:
The Vinaya experts say that this stone’s throw is characterized as up to the place where a thrown stone falls,
as, for instance, when young men exercise their arms and throw stones in order to show off their strength.
vsm1.2:48.6: But the Suttanta experts say that it is up to where one thrown to scare crows normally falls.
vsm1.2:48.7:
In the case of an unwalled village, the house precinct is where the water falls when a woman
standing in the door of the outermost house of all throws water from a basin.
vsm1.2:48.8:
Within a stone’s throw of the kind already described from that point is the village.
Within a second stone’s throw is the village precinct.
vsm1.2:49.1:
“Forest,” according to the Vinaya method firstly, is described thus:
“Except the village and its precincts, all is forest” (Vin III 46).
vsm1.2:49.2:
According to the Abhidhamma method it is described thus: “Having gone out beyond
the boundary post, all that is forest” (Vibh 251; Paṭis I 176).
vsm1.2:49.3: But according to the Suttanta method its characteristic is this: “A forest abode is five hundred bow-lengths distant” (Vin IV 183).
vsm1.2:49.4:
That should be defined by measuring it with a strung instructor’s bow from the gate-post of a walled
village, or from the range of the first stone’s throw from an unwalled one, up to the monastery wall.
vsm1.2:50.1: But if the monastery is not walled,
vsm1.2:50.2:
it is said in the Vinaya commentaries, it should be measured by making the first dwelling of all the limit, or else
the refectory or regular meeting place or Bodhi Tree or shrine, even if that is far from a dwelling belonging to the monastery.
vsm1.2:50.3:
But in the Majjhima commentary it is said that, omitting the precincts of the monastery and the village,
the distance to be measured is that between where the two stones fall.
vsm1.2:51.1:
Even if the village is close by and the sounds of men are audible to people in the monastery,
still if it is not possible to go straight to it because of rocks, rivers, etc., in between,
vsm1.2:51.2: the five hundred bow-lengths can be reckoned by that road even if one has to go by boat.
vsm1.2:51.3: But anyone who blocks the path to the village here and there
vsm1.2:51.4: for the purpose of lengthening it so as to be able to say that he is taking up the practice is cheating the ascetic practice.
vsm1.2:52.1: If a forest-dwelling bhikkhu’s preceptor or teacher is ill and does not get what he needs in the forest,
vsm1.2:52.2: he should take him to a village abode and attend him there.
vsm1.2:52.3: But he should leave in time to meet the dawn in a place proper for the practice.
vsm1.2:52.4: If the affliction increases towards the time of dawn,
vsm1.2:52.5: he must attend him and not bother about the purity of his ascetic practice. These are the directions.
vsm1.2:53.2: Herein, one who is strict must always meet the dawn in the forest.
vsm1.2:53.3: The medium one is allowed to live in a village for the four months of the Rains. And the mild one, for the winter months too.
vsm1.2:53.4:
If in the period defined any one of these three goes from the forest and hears the Dhamma in a village
abode, his ascetic practice is not broken if he meets the dawn there,
vsm1.2:53.5: nor is it broken if he meets it as he is on his way back after hearing the Dhamma.
vsm1.2:53.6: But if, when the preacher has got up, he thinks “We shall go after lying down awhile” and he meets the dawn while asleep
vsm1.2:53.7:
or if of his own choice he meets the dawn while in a village abode, then his ascetic
practice is broken. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:54.1:
The benefits are these. A forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has given attention to the perception of forest (see
MN 121) can obtain hitherto unobtained concentration, or preserve that already obtained.
vsm1.2:54.2: And the Master is pleased with him,
vsm1.2:54.3: according as it is said: “So, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest” (A III 343).
vsm1.2:54.4: And when he lives in a remote abode his mind is not distracted by unsuitable visible objects, and so on. He is free from anxiety;
vsm1.2:54.5:
he abandons attachment to life; he enjoys the taste of the bliss of seclusion,
and the state of the refuse-rag wearer, etc., becomes him.
vsm1.2:55.1:
He lives secluded and apart,
Remote abodes delight his heart;
The Saviour of the world, besides,
He gladdens that in groves abides.
vsm1.2:55.2:
The hermit that in woods can dwell
Alone, may gain the bliss as well
Whose savour is beyond the price
Of royal bliss in paradise.
vsm1.2:55.3:
Wearing the robe of rags he may
Go forth into the forest fray;
Such is his mail, for weapons too
The other practices will do.
vsm1.2:55.4:
One so equipped can be assured
Of routing Māra and his horde.
So let the forest glades delight
A wise man for his dwelling’s site.
vsm1.2:55.5: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach, and benefits, in the case of the forest-dweller’s practice.
